Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 13: x86-64 Registers
Dr. Charles Dorner

1. Read the width before interpreting the value
Problem and first experiment

SAY
A register name can describe a full value or only a portion of it. RAX names sixty-four bits, EAX the low thirty-two, AX the low sixteen, and AL the low eight. These are overlapping views, not four independent boxes. The surprising rule is that a write to EAX clears the high thirty-two bits of RAX, while ordinary writes to AX or AL preserve bits outside that narrow portion. When reading assembly, underline the destination width before predicting the next full-register value. A wrong width interpretation can change an address or a return value even when the low bits look correct.

DO
Ask which names overlap with RAX.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.006

------------------------------------------------------------

2. Model an eight-bit update without executing assembly
Problem and first experiment

SAY
The model starts with hexadecimal 1234. Masking its low byte produces decimal fifty-two because hexadecimal 34 is fifty-two. Shifting right by eight exposes decimal eighteen, which is hexadecimal 12. To model an AL write of hexadecimal AB, the program clears only the low eight bits and joins the new byte. The final printed hexadecimal value is 12ab. These operations use ordinary unsigned C++ integers; we are not reading RAX from the host processor. The point is to make the overlapping-view rule visible with exact bit operations before applying the rule to the chapter's actual assembly listing.

DO
Predict the three printed values and explain the mask.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.030

------------------------------------------------------------

3. The same bits can have different ordering
Problem and first experiment

SAY
This program interprets one eight-bit pattern in two ways. As an unsigned value, all bits set means 255, which is not less than one. As a signed eight-bit value, the same representation is minus one, which is less than one. The output therefore prints signed-less true and unsigned-less false. Bit_cast copies the representation into an equal-sized type; it is not a numeric conversion that changes the bit pattern. Fixed-width integer types make the width explicit. This safely demonstrates why a comparison needs an intended signedness. A register's bits alone do not tell a branch whether the program wanted a count or a signed temperature.

DO
Predict both Boolean outputs before running.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.028

------------------------------------------------------------

4. Register names have roles, not permanent meanings
Problem and first experiment

SAY
A disassembly does not come with permanent labels such as RSI always means a string source. Under the reference ABI, RSI commonly receives the second ordinary integer or pointer argument, but a function may reuse it after that value is no longer needed. Some instructions give particular registers implicit roles: a traditional variable shift uses CL for its count, and division uses a pair including RAX and RDX. Follow where a value is defined and where it is consumed. Historical names and entry conventions help you begin the trace, but they do not replace the current instruction's data flow.

DO
Mark the point after which an incoming argument is no longer used.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.016

5. Problem and first implementation
The chapter problem

SAY
Under x86-64 rules, writing EAX clears the upper half of RAX. Contrast this with merely replacing the low 16 bits.

Begin with the complete chapter demonstration. It fixes the input so you can follow each change in state. After that trace is clear, the lab expands the contract: Model writes of 16, 32, or 64 bits to a 64-bit x86 register. A 32-bit write clears the high half; a 16-bit write preserves the other bits. Reject unsupported widths.

6. Where the simple approach fails
The chapter problem

SAY
Applying the EAX clearing rule to AX leads to an incorrect trace. Width is part of the instruction’s meaning.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Preserve the old high half for a 32-bit write. That models an AX-like partial update, not an EAX write.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Treat width 32 as zero extension of the low 32-bit value. Test with nonzero old high bits so the distinction is observable.

7. Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
The chapter problem

SAY
The write width is part of the operation, so the function receives it explicitly instead of guessing from the numeric value. Masking the new low bits prevents them from affecting preserved bits. Rejecting widths the model does not implement is more honest than silently applying a different rule. This models ISA behavior; it does not force the compiler to use a specific register.

A plausible alternative: Inspect generated assembly when the actual register operations are the question.

8. Chapter 13 — x86-64 Registers
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Register names are a vocabulary, but register use is a contract. The ISA defines what each name designates and how instructions affect it. The ABI assigns roles at function boundaries. A register used for an argument is still a general-purpose register inside a function, provided the function respects preservation and return rules.

10. General-purpose registers
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
The baseline x86-64 general-purpose register set includes %rax , %rbx , %rcx , %rdx , %rsi , %rdi , %rsp , %rbp , and %r8 through %r15 . They can hold integer values or addresses, with some instructions imposing implicit operand roles. The ABI distinguishes caller-saved and callee-saved registers. Caller-saved values may be overwritten by a call, so a caller must preserve any such value it needs afterward. Callee-saved registers must be restored by a function that changes them. This division reduces unnecessary saving while allowing separately compiled functions to cooperate. [ R4 ]

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.004, SP13.005

11. Register widths
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A 64-bit register has narrower named views. %rax is the full 64-bit register, %eax its low 32 bits, %ax its low 16 bits, and %al its low eight bits. %ah names another eight-bit portion, but legacy high-byte registers have encoding restrictions with REX prefixes and are best avoided in beginner examples. Writing a 32-bit general-purpose register zeroes the upper 32 bits of the corresponding 64-bit register. Writing a 16-bit or eight-bit subregister generally leaves the other bits unchanged. This is why movl $1, %eax establishes a full %rax value of one, while movb $1, %al does not.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.006, SP13.007

12. %rax
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
%rax commonly carries an integer or pointer return value under the System V ABI. It is caller-saved. Some multiply and divide instructions use %rax implicitly, often together with %rdx for a double-width value. Do not assume a call preserves an unrelated value in %rax ; the callee is allowed to use it for the result and temporary work. The low byte %al also has a special role when calling variadic functions under this ABI: it conveys information about vector-register arguments. Handwritten assembly that calls a variadic library routine must follow that rule rather than only loading the visible integer arguments.

DO

13. %rbx
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
%rbx is callee-saved in the reference calling convention. A function can use it for a long-lived local value across nested calls, but must restore the caller’s original value before returning. The cost of using %rbx may include a save and restore if the function changes it. A compiler weighs that cost against repeatedly saving a caller-saved value around calls. Register allocation is therefore influenced by value lifetimes and call structure, not simply by choosing the shortest register name.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

14. %rcx
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
%rcx holds the fourth ordinary integer or pointer argument in the System V convention. It is caller-saved. The low byte %cl is also the implicit count operand for traditional variable-count shift instructions. Implicit roles can constrain instruction scheduling. A compiler may need to move a shift count into %cl even when the count originally resides elsewhere. In Linux’s x86-64 system-call ABI, the fourth argument is not passed in %rcx ; the syscall interface uses %r10 for that position. Function calls and system calls must be learned as separate interfaces.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.012, SP13.013

15. %rdx
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
%rdx carries the third ordinary integer or pointer argument and is caller-saved. It also participates in full-width multiplication and division. For signed 64-bit division, %rdx:%rax forms the signed double-width dividend, and the remainder is returned in %rdx . Before dividing a sign-extended 64-bit value, cqto prepares %rdx from the sign of %rax . Clearing %rdx instead is correct for certain unsigned dividends but wrong for a negative signed dividend. The register pair’s interpretation must match the chosen instruction.

DO

16. %rsi
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
%rsi carries the second ordinary integer or pointer argument. It is caller-saved and also has a source-index role in string instructions. Inside a function it can be reused once the argument is no longer needed. A name’s historical association is not a restriction on ordinary general-purpose use. A compiler may keep a loop bound in %rsi even when no string operation exists. Read the data flow in the current function instead of assuming the register always carries the same kind of value.

DO

17. %rdi
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
%rdi carries the first ordinary integer or pointer argument and is caller-saved. It has a destination-index role in string instructions. In a simple function taking a pointer and a length, %rdi commonly receives the pointer and %rsi the length. The first argument can also be hidden by a language ABI rule, such as a result-storage pointer or a C++ object pointer in particular cases. The simplified six-register rule is a useful starting point for ordinary scalar functions, not a complete classification algorithm for every aggregate or language feature.

18. %rsp
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
%rsp is the stack pointer. Push, pop, call, and return operations use it according to their instruction semantics. The ABI requires suitable alignment at call boundaries and restoration of the caller’s stack position before a normal return. Corrupting %rsp can redirect subsequent stack accesses and returns. Handwritten assembly must account for every push, pop, and explicit adjustment. A balanced count alone is not enough if the adjustments occur on only some control-flow paths. Trace the stack depth along every path to the return instruction.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.020, SP13.021

19. %rbp
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
%rbp is callee-saved and can serve as a frame pointer. A conventional prologue saves the old value and makes %rbp a stable reference point for the current frame. Optimized code often omits this dedicated role and uses the register for other purposes. The absence of %rbp -based accesses does not mean a function lacks local state or cannot be unwound. Debugging and exception unwinding can use metadata that describes stack changes. Conversely, having a frame pointer does not make corrupted stack contents trustworthy.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

20. %r8–%r15
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
%r8 and %r9 carry the fifth and sixth ordinary integer or pointer arguments. %r10 and %r11 are caller-saved temporaries. %r12 through %r15 are callee-saved. The narrower forms use suffixes such as %r8d , %r8w , and %r8b . These registers expand the available working set and reduce some memory spills compared with a smaller register set. They do not eliminate register pressure. Large expressions, vector work, and many simultaneously live values can still require spills to stack storage. A spill is a consequence of allocation constraints, not necessarily a sign of an incompetent compiler.

DO

21. Instruction pointer
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
%rip identifies the instruction stream position. It is not manipulated as an ordinary general-purpose destination in the same way as %rax ; control-transfer instructions and relative-addressing mechanisms provide the relevant operations. RIP-relative addressing supports position-independent access to nearby code and data. The code can refer to a symbol using a displacement that remains useful when the image is relocated. Relocations and linker decisions still matter, especially for symbols outside the current image or with different visibility.

In plain English: Think of an address written on a note: the note can tell you where to look, but it does not prove the thing is still there or that you are allowed to use it.

DO

22. Condition flags
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
The flags register includes status bits such as zero, sign, carry, and overflow. Arithmetic and comparison instructions update selected flags. Conditional branches, conditional moves, and set-on-condition instructions then interpret them. Flags do not have one universal “comparison result” meaning. Signed and unsigned order use different combinations. Carry is relevant to unsigned overflow or borrow interpretation; overflow describes signed-range overflow for particular arithmetic operations. An intervening instruction can overwrite flags, so keep the producing instruction and consuming branch connected in the data-flow analysis. [ R3 ]

In plain English: This is a coordination rule that helps multiple workers share information without stepping on each other's work.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

23. Watching partial-register writes
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Start %rax with every bit set. A 32-bit write of one clears its high half. A 16-bit write changes only the low 16 bits. An eight-bit write changes only the low byte. Companion listing: ch13/widths.S Companion listing: ch13/main.c Build on the reference platform with cc main.c widths.S -o widths . The successive full-register values are FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF , 0000000000000001 , 0000000000001234 , and 0000000000001256 . The return value verifies the final state without requiring a debugger.

24. Subregister write behavior
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
On x86-64, writing a 32-bit general-purpose subregister such as eax zero-extends into the full 64-bit register rax . Thus if rax was 0xFFFF000000000001 and an instruction writes eax = 5 , the resulting rax is 0x0000000000000005 . This differs from many 8- and 16-bit partial-register writes.

25. Following argument registers
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Under the System V AMD64 ABI, the first integer or pointer arguments are commonly passed in rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , and r9 , with integer return values in rax . A call f(10,20) therefore places the first two arguments in the first two designated registers before transferring control, unless optimization removes or transforms the call.

29. Caller-saved is permission to overwrite
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Suppose a caller leaves an important value in RAX and then calls a helper. Even if today's helper happens not to change RAX until the return, the ABI permits it to use that register for its result and temporary work. The caller must preserve any old value it still needs. Caller-saved describes that responsibility; it is not a promise that the caller always performs a save. A compiler can instead move the value to a preserved register or recompute it. This matters for maintenance because a harmless-looking helper rewrite can expose a caller that relied on behavior the interface never guaranteed.

DO
Use an old RAX value of nine and a helper return value of thirty-two.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.004

------------------------------------------------------------

30. Callee-saved means restoring the incoming value
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A callee-saved register is not reserved against use. It is available if the function restores the value it received before returning. For example, a function can save incoming RBX, use RBX to hold a loop accumulator, then restore the saved value. The saved value belongs to this caller, not to a previous call of the same function. Recursive calls therefore require independent preservation. A routine can return the correct numeric answer while still corrupting its caller by failing this obligation. Test or inspect both the result and the preserved state when reviewing assembly that participates in separately compiled software.

DO
Trace an early error return that forgets one restore.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.010

------------------------------------------------------------

31. RSP is a position that every path must repair
Reason about the implementation

SAY
The stack pointer is more than a convenient temporary register. Calls and returns use it to locate return state, and local storage relies on its current position. If one branch pushes a value but an early return skips the matching cleanup, counting one push and one pop somewhere in the function is not enough. They must balance on each actual path. The reference ABI also imposes alignment at calls, so an eight-byte change can alter whether the next call is valid. Draw stack-position changes beside the control-flow graph when debugging a routine with several exits; the register trace and branch trace must agree.

DO
Trace the stack position separately through success and error paths.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.020

------------------------------------------------------------

32. A frame pointer is optional; lifetime is not
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A conventional function uses RBP as a stable frame pointer, but optimized code may omit that role and use the register for another preserved value. This does not mean the function has no local state. Locals can be in registers, stack slots, or optimized away, and metadata can explain how to recover caller state. Likewise, the presence of a frame pointer does not extend a local array's lifetime after the function returns. Keep debugging representation separate from language lifetime. The compiler's layout choice can change without changing which borrowed references remain valid after a call boundary.

DO
Contrast logical local lifetime with an RBP-based address in one build.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.022

33. Run the complete chapter demonstration
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
Under x86-64 rules, writing EAX clears the upper half of RAX. Contrast this with merely replacing the low 16 bits.

Initial RAX. ffffffff00000000. The upper half is deliberately nonzero.

Write EAX = 7. RAX becomes 0000000000000007. A 32-bit general-register destination zero-extends on x86-64.

Instead write AX = 7. RAX becomes ffffffff00000007. A 16-bit subregister write preserves the other bits.

Build the complete demonstration and compare every output character. The separate lab solution includes assertions for its named acceptance checks.

36. Model a 32-bit register write
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
Model a 32-bit register write. Converting the unsigned 32-bit value 7 to 64 bits gives 7 with zero high bits. This models the high-half clearing caused by an x86 EAX write.

Under x86-64 rules, writing EAX clears the upper half of RAX. Contrast this with merely replacing the low 16 bits.

The upper half is deliberately nonzero. A 32-bit general-register destination zero-extends on x86-64. A 16-bit subregister write preserves the other bits.

Converting the unsigned 32-bit value 7 to 64 bits gives 7 with zero high bits. This models the high-half clearing caused by an x86 EAX write.

The mask clears only the low sixteen bits before inserting 7. The other bits of old remain, modeling an AX write. ULL supplies a sufficiently wide unsigned literal.

A modeled 32-bit write clears the high 32 bits; a modeled 16-bit write preserves the other 48 bits.

Applying the EAX clearing rule to AX leads to an incorrect trace. Width is part of the instruction’s meaning. In the extended lab: Preserve the old high half for a 32-bit write. That models an AX-like partial update, not an EAX write.

45. Review the extension solution
Practice and extension

SAY
The write width is part of the operation, so the function receives it explicitly instead of guessing from the numeric value. Masking the new low bits prevents them from affecting preserved bits. Rejecting widths the model does not implement is more honest than silently applying a different rule. This models ISA behavior; it does not force the compiler to use a specific register. Repair principle: Treat width 32 as zero extension of the low 32-bit value. Test with nonzero old high bits so the distinction is observable.

Build the complete demonstration and compare every output character. The separate lab solution includes assertions for its named acceptance checks.

47. Chapter summary and maintenance
Recall and transfer

SAY
The write width is part of the operation, so the function receives it explicitly instead of guessing from the numeric value. Masking the new low bits prevents them from affecting preserved bits. Rejecting widths the model does not implement is more honest than silently applying a different rule. This models ISA behavior; it does not force the compiler to use a specific register.

Choose a simpler approach when its narrower contract is enough. Inspect generated assembly when the actual register operations are the question.

When this system changes, retain a check that exposes the known failure: Preserve the old high half for a 32-bit write. That models an AX-like partial update, not an EAX write. Treat width 32 as zero extension of the low 32-bit value. Test with nonzero old high bits so the distinction is observable.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SYS13.14

------------------------------------------------------------

48. Flags need their own def-use trace
Recall and transfer

SAY
Register data flow includes the condition flags, even though many listings do not show them as explicit operands. A comparison establishes equality and ordering evidence. A later branch consumes particular flags according to signed or unsigned rules. Insert a zeroing XOR between them, and the branch may now read flags from the XOR instead of the comparison. That can create a control-flow bug without changing either compared register. Annotate the flag producer and consumer just as you would annotate a value written into RAX and later read. The useful unit of reasoning is the dependency, not two nearby instruction spellings.

DO
Mark a comparison-to-branch dependency and propose a safe place for unrelated work.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.028

------------------------------------------------------------

49. Translate register facts into a review checklist
Recall and transfer

SAY
When handed a short assembly routine, begin with its declared C signature and target ABI. Identify which argument values enter which registers and which result width the caller expects. Then track narrow writes, signed comparisons, implicit operands, and values that remain live across calls. Do not carry the ordinary fourth-argument RCX rule into a Linux x86-64 system-call wrapper, where that position uses R10. The chapter's register names become useful when tied to these boundaries. A compact table supports memory, but a full explanation must show what each register means at a particular point in the actual routine.

DO
Ask for a register trace before allowing an optimization suggestion.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch13.json → SP13.036
